title: Convert the greenhouse thermometers
problem: Botie's greenhouses record Celsius, but the display expects Fahrenheit. We need to convert each reading while preserving its greenhouse position.
challenge: Build a Celsius-to-Fahrenheit converter. Multiply each reading by 1.8, then add 32. It must work on every supplied list.
why: Each wire still carries one entry per greenhouse. The multiplication changes the degree size; the addition changes the reference point.
limitation: This is a unit conversion, not a fitted prediction rule.

title: Keep each greenhouse's average
problem: Botie wants to compare greenhouses over several days. Our rows are days, so a row average would answer a different question.
challenge: Build one average per greenhouse. You can swap the table's rows and columns, then average within each resulting row.
why: Swapping rows and columns puts one greenhouse's readings together. Each row average then keeps that greenhouse separate.
limitation: All days receive equal weight, and every greenhouse has a reading on every day.

title: Prepare the greenhouse target sheet
problem: Botie needs a target for each day and greenhouse before recording comparisons.
challenge: Choose a tool to create a rectangular sheet using the supplied day count, greenhouse count, and target. Then subtract the supplied readings from those targets to find how much warmer each position would need to become.
why: The shape comes from the requested report. The filled sheet supplies references, while subtraction compares them with actual observations.
limitation: The workshop uses small positive dimensions. It does not expose uninitialised storage.

title: Retrieve the requested mornings
problem: Botie saved the row numbers needed for a comparison. The output must preserve the requested order and repeated requests.
challenge: Gather the requested day rows, then swap rows and columns so each output row follows one greenhouse through those requested days.
why: Gather chooses the days; transpose changes which meaning occupies a row. Neither step averages or sorts the selected temperatures.
limitation: These workshop wires carry values rather than shared NumPy storage. Copy and view behaviour is demonstrated and checked in Python.

title: Recover the greenhouse columns from a logger stream
problem: Botie's flat logger output contains complete days in sequence. We need one row per greenhouse for a comparison over time.
challenge: Group the sequence into day rows using the supplied number of greenhouses, then swap axes to follow each greenhouse.
why: Grouping restores the day boundaries. Transpose then follows greenhouse identity across those days.
limitation: The logger order and row width are supplied. The construction cannot infer missing labels or repair an incomplete day.

title: Compare greenhouse readings with their targets
problem: Botie needs the difference from each greenhouse's target on every day. The target order matches the greenhouse columns.
challenge: Subtract one target per greenhouse from every day's readings. Preserve both the day rows and greenhouse columns.
why: Each target stays attached to its column as the rows pass through the calculation.
limitation: The workshop tool handles a reference vector across rows. It does not implement every possible NumPy broadcasting pattern.

title: Find the greenhouse alerts
problem: Botie needs the readings at or above the chosen limit. We should keep the measurements that satisfy the rule, not multiply them by the limit.
challenge: Build a mask using the threshold, then use it to select the original readings. Preserve their order and allow an empty result.
why: The comparison makes the decisions; selection applies those decisions to the original temperatures.
limitation: The limit is supplied by the task. It is not a learned or medically meaningful threshold.

title: Order the inspection report without losing its names
problem: Botie wants the greenhouse names from coolest to warmest. Sorting names alphabetically would detach them from the temperatures.
challenge: Find the ascending order of the readings, then use those indices to retrieve the names.
why: One ordering is computed from measurements and applied to their labels. Stable ties keep the earlier report order.
limitation: Ordering is not a measure of danger. These temperatures only illustrate preserving aligned records.

title: Inspect every error before summarising the report
problem: Botie wants one average squared deviation from a supplied target. Opposite temperature deviations must not cancel.
challenge: Subtract the target from each reading, square the individual differences, then average their contributions.
why: Each reading contributes before the reduction. The construction exposes the intermediate array so a cancellation mistake is visible.
limitation: The target is supplied. This example evaluates a fixed reference rather than learning a prediction rule.

title: Apply a rule to the greenhouse feature table
problem: Botie has one feature row per greenhouse and one coefficient per feature. We need a score for every row.
challenge: Apply the coefficient vector to each row, adding its weighted contributions, then add the supplied offset.
why: Matrix times vector collects each row's weighted contributions. The offset applies to every resulting score.
limitation: The coefficients are supplied. Python separately introduces exact solving and least-squares fitting.

title: Check the largest recovery error
problem: Botie has original and recovered temperatures in matching order. Every recovered value must be within a supplied absolute tolerance.
challenge: Find the absolute difference at each position, then its largest value. Return 1 if that largest error is no greater than the tolerance, otherwise 0.
why: The largest error represents the worst entry. Putting tolerance first in the threshold comparison includes equality at the boundary.
limitation: Workshop inputs are finite, equally sized vectors. Python adds shape, dtype, missing-value, and relative-tolerance checks.

title: Replay a recorded greenhouse sample
problem: Botie has saved the indices from a resample. We need to retrieve those readings, including repeats, and calculate their average.
challenge: Gather the readings at the supplied zero-based indices, then return the mean of that selected list.
why: Gather preserves the recorded choices. The mean describes that resample, so changing the indices can change the result even when the underlying report stays the same.
limitation: The indices are supplied. This construction does not generate randomness or establish that a sample is representative.

title: Reuse the training reference on another report
problem: Botie wants a new report described relative to the training average. Replacing that average with the new report's average would change the comparison.
challenge: Calculate the mean of the training readings, subtract it from the new report, and collect the reference and transformed report together in that order.
why: The same fitted reference explains every output. Collecting both results mirrors a function returning its reference and transformed array.
limitation: Workshop cases satisfy the finite, nonempty vector contract. Python is where we define functions and handle invalid inputs.

title: Recompute scores from a restored report
problem: Botie has already loaded the saved feature table, coefficient vector, and greenhouse names. We need to check that those pieces still work together.
challenge: Compute one weighted score per restored feature row, then collect the scores and the names together, scores first.
why: The restored coefficients produce one score per row, and the restored names retain the row identity.
limitation: The workshop starts after loading and checks how the restored data is used. The Python examples and challenges perform the actual file-format round trips in memory.

title: Fill a greenhouse report from its training reference
problem: Botie's report has absent temperatures. Learn a replacement from observed training readings, then fill only the missing report entries.
challenge: Select the observed training values, find their mean, and use that mean to replace blanks in the new report.
why: The training branch supplies one reference. The report branch retains its measurements and uses that reference only at absent entries.
limitation: Mean replacement is a baseline. It cannot recover the true missing values or represent uncertainty about them.

title: Represent the greenhouse roof materials
problem: Botie needs a stable numerical description of roof material without treating an arbitrary ID as a quantity. We will build the three indicator columns separately, then arrange them into rows.
challenge: Read each of the three vocabulary entries by its zero-based index. Compare all materials with each entry to make a column of indicators. Collect the first two columns, append the third column, then swap rows and columns so each material has one row. Unknown materials receive all zeros.

sources.vocabulary: Three training categories in fixed order

why: Each comparison builds a separate category column. Collecting and transposing those columns puts one material's answers together in each row.
limitation: This construction uses exactly three vocabulary categories so the comparisons remain visible. It does not fit a model or remove redundant columns.

title: Give the greenhouse clock two coordinates
problem: Botie's hour feature should preserve that the day repeats. We will return the position around a circle, with cosine first and sine second.
challenge: Divide the hour by the period, multiply by a full turn of 2π radians, then collect cosine and sine in that order. The Full turn source supplies 2π.
why: Dividing identifies the fraction of a cycle. Sine and cosine locate that fraction on a circle, so a full turn returns to the start.
limitation: This encodes a fixed-period feature. It does not fit a temperature curve or handle calendar irregularities.

title: Audit repeated greenhouse events
problem: Botie combined sensor exports that may overlap. Each stable ID names one event, so extra copies should be counted before analysis.
challenge: Return the number of imported rows beyond the number of distinct event IDs.
why: The two branches count all records and distinct identities. Subtracting them measures extra copies rather than genuine repeated values.
limitation: This audit assumes IDs identify events reliably. It does not decide which conflicting record should be kept.

title: Reconstruct the prediction-time report
problem: Botie must predict repair need using only evidence available at the decision time. Later measurements remain in the export but cannot enter this prediction.
challenge: Build an availability mask that includes times at or before the cutoff, then select the corresponding measurements.
why: The gate compares the cutoff with each availability time. Selection keeps only the measurements whose evidence was available then.
limitation: Times are simplified whole hours. A real system also needs dates, time zones, ingestion delays, and update history.

title: Keep the rare sensor failures visible
problem: Botie needs a score that gives each sensor class a place. Compute each class's recall before combining the results.
challenge: Divide the correct count for each class by that class's total count, then return the mean of those recalls.
why: Division makes class-specific recall. Averaging those recalls gives each class equal weight in the summary.
limitation: All supplied class counts are positive. Balanced accuracy does not encode application-specific mistake costs.

title: Measure the greenhouse baseline
problem: Botie needs a reference score before adding a more complicated temperature model. Fit one constant on training data and evaluate it on the held-out temperatures.
challenge: Compute the training mean, subtract the held-out answers, square the differences, and return their mean.
why: The training branch supplies the prediction. Only the scoring branch reads the held-out answers.
limitation: This baseline uses no input features. Its score is a comparison, not a guarantee of acceptable temperature prediction.

title: Compare the two greenhouse error curves
problem: Botie has training and validation errors for matching training sizes. We need to see their differences without confusing a narrow gap with low error.
challenge: Return validation error minus training error at every supplied training size, preserving the order.
why: Each subtraction compares the same training size. Read these gaps beside the error levels before deciding what to try next.
limitation: These errors are supplied teaching illustrations. No model is fitted by this construction.

title: Turn failure probabilities into inspection decisions
problem: Botie has failure probabilities and a simplified cost table. Correct decisions cost zero; false alarms and missed failures have the supplied costs.
challenge: Derive the cutoff as false-alarm cost divided by the sum of both costs. Return one or zero for each probability, inspecting at equality.
why: The costs determine a cutoff. The gate then turns each supplied probability into an action under that rule.
limitation: This assumes credible probabilities, nonnegative costs with a positive sum, and zero cost for correct decisions. Different cost tables require a different derivation.

title: Audit one group of failure probabilities
problem: Botie needs to compare the group's confidence with its observed failure rate, while also reporting squared probability error.
challenge: Return two entries: first a pair containing mean probability and observed failure frequency, then the Brier score. Outcomes are zero or one.
why: The first pair compares probability with frequency. The separate score reports average squared error without pretending it measures calibration alone.
limitation: These tiny groups illustrate the arithmetic. They do not estimate calibration precisely or fit a correction.

title: Audit the held-out greenhouses
problem: Botie needs to know whether any greenhouse appears on both sides of a proposed split. Repeated rows must not count the same overlapping greenhouse more than once.
challenge: Keep distinct IDs on each side, compare their memberships, and count the shared identities. Return zero only when there is no overlap.
why: Distinct IDs remove repeated records from the audit. Each remaining match identifies one greenhouse shared by both sets.
limitation: This checks the supplied group identity only. It cannot discover hidden relationships or incorrectly assigned IDs.

title: Compare the greenhouse population mix
problem: Botie needs to compare roof-category shares in a reference report and a new report. Both use the same category order.
challenge: Normalise each count vector by its own total, take absolute differences, add them, and divide by two.
why: Normalisation removes volume differences. The remaining distance measures how the supplied category shares differ.
limitation: Both reports must have positive totals and aligned, nonnegative counts. This is a distribution audit, not a performance estimate or an automatic retraining rule.

title: Recalculate a resampled greenhouse mean
problem: Botie has a recorded bootstrap draw. Retrieve its observations with replacement and calculate the estimate for that draw.
challenge: Gather the supplied positions from the original readings, including repeats, then calculate their mean.
why: The resample changes which observed values contribute and how often. Recalculating the mean turns that changed composition into one estimate.
limitation: The construction receives a fixed draw and performs no random sampling. A few illustrative means are not a confidence interval.
